name: speedread
desc: Simple terminal-based rapid serial visual presentation (RSVP) reader
why: A terminal RSVP reader that flashes words at you, a small but strange look at how reading can be sped up.

brief.what_it_is: speedread is a terminal command-line filter that displays input text one word at a time using RSVP (rapid serial visual presentation), with each word aligned on a fixed reading point. You pipe text in, for example with cat, and the words flash in the terminal at a set speed. The default is 250 words per minute, and the README suggests raising it. Its controls are [ and ] to slow down or speed up by 10%, and space to pause and show the last two lines of context.
brief.why_it_exists: The README says RSVP lets you read much faster than usual because your eye can stay fixed on one spot instead of scanning lines. It is described as an open source Spritz-alike, a nod to the commercial Spritz reader.
brief.how_it_works: It reads text from standard input and shows it word by word at the chosen words-per-minute rate. Each word is aligned on what the README calls optimal reading points, the position where the eye best recognises it. Pauses are longer at commas and full stops. The README's TODO list admits the timing is crude, since short words like "not" and "can" can get missed.

commands_seen.context: Basic example from the README: pipes a text file into speedread and sets the speed to 250 words per minute, the default, which the README calls timid.
Mutt macro line to put in ~/.muttrc. Press R in the pager to pipe the current message, with quoted lines removed by grep, into speedread.

brief.install_notes: The README gives no build or install steps and names no dependencies or runtime. Its examples run ./speedread from a checkout, so the brew-installed binary on PATH is the one to use. The mutt recipe assumes the script sits at ~/speedread/speedread. No accounts or special hardware are mentioned.
brief.standout: It is a Unix-filter take on Spritz: it takes plain text on stdin and works as a pipe target, so it fits into mail clients and other tools. The README also shows an elinks recipe as a TODO, which points to web pages being read the same way.
brief.status: unknown. The README has no release dates, changelog, or version information, and I did not check the commit history. The TODO list says "Not sure if I will ever get around to these...", which suggests the author is not actively planning new work.
brief.caveats: The README says the mutt recipe does not work with non-ASCII messages, probably because of mutt limitations. The timing is simplistic and the author lists better word timing as a TODO. Seeking back and forward is not implemented. Configurable timing and ORP coefficients are also TODO. No license is mentioned in the README I read.
quotes: A simple terminal-based open source Spritz-alike.
The default of 250 words per minute is very timid, designed so that you get used to this.
Unfortunately, it does not work with non-ASCII messages (probably due to mutt limitations).
